are responsible for the accurate documentation of completed coursework on their
transcript. Concerns or discrepancies should be reported to the school counselor.

courses.description: Structured Literacy is a semester-long course that employs a systematic instructional approach to the five fundamental skills of reading: Phonemic Awareness - the ability to distinguish individual sounds within spoken words; Phonics - the connection of a speech sound (phoneme) with its representative written symbol (grapheme); Vocabulary and Language Comprehension - a primary determinant of reading comprehension; Reading Fluency - the ability to read with sufficient accuracy, rate, and expression to support comprehension; and Reading Comprehension - the ultimate purpose and goal for reading. Our main curricular resources are the Orton-Gillingham literacy approach, Framing Your Thoughts, Self-Regulated Strategy Development, and The Writing Revolution. Students will progress through the curriculum at a pace commensurate with their mastery of concepts, and may take multiple levels of this course.
courses.notes: Intended Grade Level: As needed by placement; Heading says Year Long; description calls it semester-long

courses.description: Structured Literacy 2 is a semester-long course that is a continuation of Structured Literacy I. The instruction focuses on providing explicit, systematic, and cumulative instruction in literacy skills with a heavy focus on morphology, syntax, and semantics. Instruction in vocabulary development and comprehension strategies are provided to support reading fluency and comprehension at the high school level.
courses.notes: Intended Grade Level: As needed by placement; Heading says Year Long; description calls it semester-long

courses.description: In this course, you will explore a systematic approach to the writing process, starting with an emphasis on spoken language and culminating in essay writing. We will adhere to the structured framework provided by Self-Regulated Strategy Development and The Writing Revolution for our language and writing instruction. Throughout the curriculum, students will engage in discussions, readings, and writing activities centered around high school-level history and science content, ensuring a comprehensive learning experience.
courses.notes: Intended Grade Level: As needed by placement

courses.description: Freshman English is a semester-long survey course designed to ensure a productive and successful transition to high school, along with providing a solid foundation for high school English. Through the study of literature, informational text, and digital media, students will explore major themes and essential questions about the human condition over a broad period of time across the globe. Students will have opportunities to practice and demonstrate proficiency in skills and content area standards, including reading, writing, speaking and listening, presentation, and language.

courses.notes: Intended Grade Level: 10 or higher who failed ENG121A

courses.description: In Sophomore English, students will engage in study that focuses on grade-level expectations. Students will discuss, analyze, and reflect on a variety of genres, including fiction, drama, and memoir. All units will include a reading component, formal and informal writing, oral presentations, and critical thinking assignments, which will all be united by a thematic quest for identity.

Journalism I is a semester course designed for students interested in developing their writing skills and learning about the ever-evolving world of media. This course explores news writing and editing; the rights and ethical responsibilities of a journalist; and the power of the written word in modern society. Throughout this course, students will have the opportunity to research, write, and edit original articles using a variety of news structures. Students taking this course will be expected to complete all class readings, hold discussions, and give presentations on a range of journalistic topics.
courses.prerequisites: English I and II

courses.description: In this course, we will explore Gothic literature and its influence on the mystery and horror genres. Through close examinations of several texts, we will identify the unique aspects of each genre in addition to their commonalities. Beware of ghosts, murderers, monsters, and the limits of humanity, as we seek to understand all things that go bump in the night.
courses.prerequisites: English I and II

courses.description: In this course, students will read, analyze, and evaluate myths from around the world. We will consider the ways myths reflect the unique culture in which they were created, as well as sharing common themes and patterns across cultures and time periods. Additionally, students will examine the role and influence of mythology on contemporary literature and film. Units will include reading, speaking, and listening components, formal and informal writing and presentations. Students will also participate in weekly vocabulary and grammar instruction.
courses.prerequisites: English I and II

courses.description: This course focuses on the literature of genocide, beginning with World War II and including previous and subsequent acts of genocide. Students will engage with a variety of texts including first-person accounts, poetry, film, and historical fiction to gain a deeper understanding of the emotional and psychological costs of these byproducts of war. Units will include reading, speaking and listening components, formal and informal writing, and presentations.
courses.prerequisites: English I and II

courses.description: This semester-long intervention course reinforces and continues the development of reading, writing, speaking, and listening skills. Through close reading, interactive discussion, and type II writes, students will examine real-life themes such as wellness, family dynamics, and learning challenges. Encountering new vocabulary, students will continue to develop context reading skills and comprehension of words and phrases by discovering meaning and applying knowledge to practical situations. Ultimately, students will connect themes discussed throughout the semester to draft, revise, and develop explanatory and argument essays.
courses.notes: Intended Grade Level: 11, 12 as needed by placement

courses.description: Modern American Voices focuses on literature written in the U.S. from the middle of the twentieth-century to recent times. Works are chosen to represent diverse ethnic, racial, and social groups in historical, political, and economic contexts for what they reflect and reveal about the evolving American experience and character. Units will include reading, speaking, and listening components, formal and informal writing and presentations. Students will also participate in weekly vocabulary and grammar instruction.
courses.prerequisites: English I and II

courses.description: This course examines the literary genre of the graphic novel, which, like all comics, juxtaposes words and images to convey a story, whether fiction or nonfiction. Graphic novels typically address complex and challenging issues and topics, such as violence, trauma, sexuality, gender, and race. We will look at the narrative techniques and forms specific to the genre and the broader history of comics and visual narrative in order to better understand the place of the graphic novel within that history. Thematic links among the primary texts will speak to issues of cultural memory, nostalgia, and identity.
courses.prerequisites: English I and II

courses.description: In Social Issues in Literature, students will expand their understanding of basic human rights by examining works of fiction and nonfiction. As students explore themes including the ways people dehumanize others and what it means to be human, they will complete written and online responses and participate in classroom discussion. Key units will include refugee experiences, hate crimes, and domestic violence. Students will be expected to successfully complete a guided independent project on a topic of their choice.
courses.prerequisites: English I and II

courses.description: Students will examine and explore various themes and concepts of war, including but not limited to the issues of war, the men and women involved in war conflict, the families left behind, the innocent victims of war, and war itself. In addition, students will explore social and historical issues pertaining to war, including “just war” principles and the tactics of war. The course will include the reading and discussion of nonfiction, fiction, and poetry, as well as oral histories and some film study.

This course will examine the popular genre of dystopian fiction with a focus on understanding its purpose and relevance in today’s world. Students will be introduced to key terms and concepts of the genre, including the characteristics of dystopian societies, the general warnings inherent in them, and the broad trends in dystopias over time. Units will include reading, speaking, and listening components, formal and informal writing, and presentations. Students will also participate in weekly vocabulary and grammar instruction.
courses.prerequisites: English I and II

courses.description: This course introduces students to a variety of works of literature primarily published in this century. Through readings in long and short fiction and poetry, students explore the range of human experience across national and cultural boundaries. The primary focus is on diverse and multicultural texts. Through the literature of contemporary writers from around the world, students can gain a broader and deeper understanding of a variety of experiences. This course is considered a "concurrent class", as this is a CCV(Community College of Vermont)-approved course, taught by a Spaulding High School teacher, and during the regular high school day. A dual enrollment voucher is required to be used to access this course. Should a student desire to take this course, but has already used both of their Dual Enrollment vouchers, a small fee will be required to be paid by the student/family to participate in this college course. Additionally, students will need to meet CCV's requirements in order to be placed in this course.
courses.prerequisites: Acceptance to CCV as a Dual Enrollment Student. Students should show evidence by earning 3.5 or higher in English 10, US History or their equivalent and Department Chair approval. Note: this course has an attendance requirement

courses.description: In this course, students develop effective composition skills and research techniques. Students learn strategies for organizing, evaluating, and revising their work through extensive reading of a variety of essay styles and literary texts; apply writing and research techniques to their papers; and demonstrate proficiency in first-year college-level writing and information literacy. This course is considered a "concurrent class", as this is a CCV(Community College of Vermont)-approved course, taught by a Spaulding High School teacher, and during the regular high school day. A dual enrollment voucher is required to be used to access this course. Should a student desire to take this course, but has already used both of their Dual Enrollment vouchers, a small fee will be required to be paid by the student/family to participate in this college course. Additionally, students will need to meet CCV's requirements in order to be placed in this course.
courses.prerequisites: Acceptance to CCV as a Dual Enrollment Student. Students should show evidence by earning 3.5 or higher in English 10, US History or their equivalent and Department Chair approval. Note: this course has an attendance requirement

courses.description: This course is designed to introduce students to the techniques used in rhetorical composition. The course focuses primarily on nonfiction writing and American literature selections. Fiction and nonfiction are used to examine how authors use linguistic choices to achieve a desired effect. Each unit is organized in two ways. First, a theme ties the unit texts and images. Secondly—and more specifically—a rhetorical focus establishes students' interaction with nonfiction texts and images throughout the unit. *Students are required to take the Advanced Placement English Language and Composition exam in May.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of grade 9 & 10 English or their equivalents. If you wish to take this course as a junior, it is recommended that you have earned a 3.3 or higher in both your Sophomore English and US History courses. If you have not achieved these grades students should meet with the instructor for permission.

courses.description: AP English Literature is a college-level literature and composition class. Students will read poetry, fiction, and drama from British, American and world literature. The class is conducted as a seminar; students should be willing to think aloud and engage in discussion with a partner, a small group, and the entire class. They will write regularly in class and should be prepared to share their work.. Formal essay assignments on major works will further develop students’ skills in analysis and interpretation. There will be several projects/presentations. Students will also study vocabulary and grammar.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of grade 9 & 10 English or their equivalents. If you wish to take this course as a junior, it is recommended that you have earned a 3.3 or higher in both your Sophomore English and US History courses. If you have not achieved these grades students should meet with the instructor for permission.

courses.description: In this course, students develop key algebraic concepts in a rapid succession through explorations and investigations using technology. A potential honors student should be able to skillfully handle the arithmetic of whole numbers, fractions, decimals and percents without a calculator and perform tasks within time limits. Students need to have a significant degree of motivation to be successful in this course.
courses.prerequisites: Placement by Math Department

courses.description: In this course, students examine such topics as proportions, direct variation, linear equations, systems of equations, and inequalities. The examination of the topics are embedded in real-life situations and applications, and includes investigations where students construct their own understanding of the mathematical concepts. A potential Algebra student should also be able to follow directions and be disciplined to read, listen and think. To be successful the student must complete daily assignments and be able to work cooperatively in groups as well as independently. To assist students to be more successful, more time is given for the learning experience.
courses.prerequisites: Placement by Math Department or completion of Foundations

courses.description: This course works to support students to reinforce and build upon existing knowledge of numbers as well as encourage the use of calculators, making drawings, and asking questions to approach problems. The curriculum is a mix of probability, fractions, proportions, variables, percents, angles and geometric figures. Work is primarily done in class as the purpose of this course is to build and strengthen classroom and mathematical habits around discussion, questioning and work in order to assist students in growing their own mathematical skills. A Connections student will need to work with other students to solve problems and discuss ideas.
courses.prerequisites: Placement by Math Department

courses.description: For some students, this will be an entry-level course and for others it will be a continuation from their work in Connections. Students examine such topics as integers, equations, probability, patterns, order of operations, ratios and proportions, percent applications, Pythagorean Theorem, area and volume. Work from the beginning of the course builds throughout the course, continuously reinforcing earlier strategies. A potential Foundations student may need additional skill development in basic computation and/or a more concrete understanding of mathematical concepts generally presented in high school math courses. To be successful, a Foundations student must complete daily assignments and work cooperatively with their peers. To assist students in developing mathematical understanding and reasoning skills, the course extends through the year and prepares students for discovering Algebra.
courses.prerequisites: Placement by Math Department or completion of Connections
courses.notes: Intended Grade Level: 9, 10; Shared description with Foundations (Grade 10 / Grade 9 only)
