To assist students in developing mathematical understanding and reasoning skills, the course extends through the year and prepares students for discovering Algebra.
courses.prerequisites: Placement by Math Department or completion of Connections
courses.notes: Intended Grade Level: 9, 10; Shared description with Foundations (Grade 10 / Grade 9 only)

courses.description: In this course, students follow the logical development of the structure of Euclidean Geometry, with an emphasis on problem solving involving planes and solid figures. It is a challenging course for students with a high degree of motivation to devote to daily preparedness and perseverance. Students must have the ability to read, understand, and apply the concepts presented. There is a rapid progression of topics and students must be able to perform within time limits.
courses.prerequisites: Must earn 2.8 or higher in Algebra I Honors or 3.5 or higher in Algebra I Part A and B and/or placement by Math Department

courses.description: In Geometry, students examine such topics as area, volume, geometric constructions, triangle properties, different forms of reasoning, similarity, and trigonometry. The examination of these topics is embedded in real-life situations such as surveying and architecture. This includes investigations, where students use inductive reasoning to form their own understanding of the mathematical concept. A potential geometry student should be skilled in basic computation and algebra skills and have the willingness and ability to read, listen, and think. Geometry students must also work in groups and independently, and complete daily assignments to be successful.
courses.prerequisites: Must earn credit Algebra I A & B or Financial Algebra

courses.description: This course is a continuation of Algebra I Honors, with an emphasis on problem solving using algebraic concepts. Students must be highly motivated with a solid understanding of previous math courses, be able to think abstractly and be proficient problem solvers. There is a rapid progression of topics and students must be able to perform within time limits.
courses.prerequisites: Must earn 3.0 or higher or better in Honors Algebra1 and 2.8 or higher in Honors Geometry, or 3.5 or higher in Algebra 1B and Geometry and placement by Math Department

courses.description: This is a one-semester course with a rapid progression of topics such as: recursion, functions, relations, transformations, exponential and logarithmic properties, composite and inverse functions, higher degree polynomials and quadratics. The examination of these topics is embedded in real life situations such as projectile motion and modeling. To be successful students must complete daily work and be disciplined to read, listen, and think independently.
courses.prerequisites: Must earn 2.8 or higher in Geometry and Algebra 1B or honors Algebra or department permission.

courses.description: This is an advanced one-semester course for the motivated mathematics student. It is designed to prepare students for post-secondary education. Topics include: functions, mathematical models, periodic functions, trigonometric and circular functions, trigonometric identities, combinations of sinusoids, conic sections, polynomial and rational functions, limits, and an introduction to derivatives. The examination of these topics are presented graphically, algebraically, verbally and numerically. To be successful students must complete daily assignments.
courses.prerequisites: Must earn 2.8 in Algebra II Honors or 3.0 in Algebra II and/or placement by Math Department

courses.description: Statistics is a one-semester course for the college bound student interested in pursuing a wide variety of majors including math/science (math, engineering, etc.), business and social sciences (economics, psychology, etc). The goals of this course are to further the knowledge and usage of statistics regarding organizing and producing data, probability and inference. This course moves quickly and assumes knowledge of Algebra 1, Algebra 2 and Geometry topics and uses a variety of learning methods including explorations, experiments and self-directed study. There is a heavy dependence on the TI-83 series calculator. To be successful, Statistics students must complete daily work and read, listen, and think independently. Embedded honors option available.
courses.prerequisites: Must earn credit in Algebra II Honors or Algebra II and/or placement by Math Department

courses.description: This course provides an introduction to programming and robotics through a series of individual and team based design activities and labs. Students will develop key engineering and programming skills in the field of robotics. This includes learning about the design and iterative process, written and block programming, systems and controllers and how mathematics, science and statistics apply to engineering. Students will practice and be assessed on written and oral communication, teamwork, and management of short and long term projects. The course integrates mathematics, coding in multiple languages, building and engineering principles. Students should have a solid understanding of Algebra and geometry in order to code more complex tasks and solve challenges with a robotic system.
courses.prerequisites: Must earn credit for Algebra IB or instructor's permission

courses.description: This Introduction to design course provides an introduction to engineering through a series of team-based design projects. Drawing from a diverse set of engineering problems, students will design and build a variety of structures. Students will practice written and oral communication, teamwork, and management of long-term team-based projects. The course integrates mathematics and some science with a variety of types of engineering to provide students with a solid introduction to the engineering field.
courses.prerequisites: Credit for Geometry or Geometry Honors

courses.description: An introductory course designed to develop logical reasoning and computer programming skills through immersion in the fundamentals of a programming language. Programming projects involving mathematical problems and logic games challenge students to develop their logical reasoning, systematic thinking, and problem-solving skills. Students become familiar with fundamental object-oriented programming concepts, algorithms, and techniques. This course covers an overview of introductory material through hands-on labs and individual and collaborative projects. Embedded honors option available.
courses.prerequisites: Must earn credit for Algebra IB or Honors Algebra or instructor's permission

courses.description: This Advanced Placement Calculus course is taught at the college level and covers the topics of the first semester of college calculus, including limits, derivatives, definite integrals and indefinite integrals. This is a full year course. A successful Calculus student will be self-disciplined, think independently, and be able to complete timed assessments in preparation for the AP Exam. *Students are required to take the national Advanced Placement Calculus AB Exam in May and to have a graphing calculator on the approved list. Curriculum is defined by the AP program, which includes differential and integral calculus with a focus on problem-solving and applications.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Pre-Calculus Honors

courses.description: This course is a continuation of MAT403-Statistics that covers new topics and reviews key areas in preparation for the AP Exam. This Advanced Placement class is taught at the college level and covers the first semester of college Statistics. *Students are required to take the national Advanced Placement Exam in May and to have a graphing calculator on the approved list. Curriculum is defined by the AP Program. A successful AP Statistics student will be self-disciplined, think independently, and be able to complete timed assessments in preparation for the AP Exam.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Statistics or Instructor Permission

courses.description: This Advanced Placement Calculus course is taught at the college level and covers the topics of the first two semesters of college calculus, including limits, derivatives, definite integrals, indefinite integrals, parametric functions, polar functions, vector topics, polynomial approximations and series. Curriculum is defined by the AP program which includes differential and integral calculus with a focus on problem-solving and applications. This is a full year course. A successful Calculus student will be self-disciplined, think independently, and be able to complete timed assessments in preparation for the AP Exam. *Students are required to take the national Advanced Placement Calculus BC Exam in May and to have a graphing calculator on the approved list.
courses.prerequisites: Must earn 3.2 or higher in Algebra II and Pre-Calculus. Honors and/or placement by the Math Department

courses.description: Physical Science is a foundational course where students learn the basics of chemistry, earth science, and climate sciences in a student centered, investigative, and skill-based way. Students will participate in learning that focuses on the skills used in science. Also students will explore science through a phenomenon based, method of science learning where they are presented with observable, real world events with an inherent problem, issue or mystery that needs to be solved. Students will study concepts such as thermodynamics in the earth system, the structure of the properties of matter, molecular processes in the earth’s system, and chemical reactions in our world. They will be faced with real world issues like how to solve problems from sea level rise from global melting in an arctic community by the sea, what causes lightning and what buildings are safe from it, and how can we find the resources we need to live off of earth. Class will involve laboratory investigations, data collection and analysis, modeling activities, whole-class and small group learning activities, and student presentations. Embedded Honors option available. Students seeking honors recognition will need to meet all required course standards as well as complete additional assessments outside of class.

Life Science is a foundational course where students are introduced to biology related concepts in a student centered, investigative, and skill-based way. Students will participate in learning that focuses on the skills used in science. Also students will explore science through a phenomenon based approach method of science learning where they are presented with observable, real world events with an inherent problem, issue or mystery that needs to be solved. . Students will work toward standards that focus on improving students' ability to investigate how living things and the environment are interconnected. Topics studied will include ecosystem interactions and dynamics, inheritance and genetic variation, natural selection and evolution. They will be faced with real world issues like how to solve problems from habitat loss, the prevention and treatment of cancer, how organisms evolve and are affected by climate change , and how to design solutions for urban growth to balance protecting biodiversity with human needs in the area. Class will involve laboratory investigations, data collection and analysis, modeling activities, whole-class and small group learning activities, and student presentations. Embedded Honors option available. Students seeking honors recognition will need to meet all required course standards as well as complete additional assessments outside of class.
courses.prerequisites: Physical Science

courses.description: This college preparatory course introduces students to the basic laws of force, linear and circular motion, conservation of energy, momentum and torque. This course is strongly recommended for students pursuing future studies in a science or engineering field. Since the physics problems and their solutions are an integral part of the course, students need a strong background in mathematics. Embedded Honors option available. Students seeking honors recognition will need to meet all required course standards as well as complete additional assessments outside of class.
courses.prerequisites: Physical Science, Life Science, Geometry, Algebra II (honors track only)

courses.description: This college-preparatory lab science course is an introduction to interactions of matter and energy and is designed for the highly motivated student considering a career in science. Included in the content of the course are topics such as structure and properties of matter, chemical reactions, conservation of matter, stoichiometry, and energy in chemical processes. These topics are studied both qualitatively and quantitatively through lectures, laboratory investigations, and problem-solving. This course should be selected by students planning to further their education in the fields of engineering, mathematics, medicine, or the sciences. Students seeking honors recognition will need to meet all required course standards as well as complete additional assignments and assessments outside of class. Embedded Honors option available. Students seeking honors recognition will need to meet all required course standards as well as complete additional assessments outside of class.
courses.prerequisites: Physical Science, Life Science, Algebra I

courses.description: Marine biology is the scientific study of marine life and its relationship to the dynamics of the physical and chemical ocean. This course will include an introduction to oceanography as well as a study of marine plants, animals, the factors affecting their environments, and the impacts humans have on the ocean. This course is strongly recommended for students interested in pursuing a career in wildlife biology, zoology, fish & fisheries biology, marine biology, conservation biology, marine biotechnology, or aquarium technician science. Lab investigations include the research, set up and running of a freshwater aquarium, dissections and microscope activities to study anatomy, and possible field trips to New England aquarium and Roxbury Fish Hatchery. Embedded Honors option available. Students seeking honors recognition will need to meet all required course standards as well as complete additional assessments outside of class.
courses.prerequisites: Physical Science, Life Science

courses.description: Forensic Science is the application of science to those criminal and civil laws that are enforced by police agencies in a criminal justice system. This course is strongly recommended for students interested in pursuing a career in the medical or law enforcement field. It involves all areas of science including biology, anatomy, chemistry, physics, and earth science with an emphasis on complex reasoning and critical thinking. Specific topics will include: Ballistics, Blood Spatter, Fingerprinting, DNA Profiling, Forensic Entomology, Forensic Anthropology, Crime Scene Investigation, Counterfeiting and Forgeries, Drugs and Toxicology, Cause and Manner of Death. Students will engage in lectures, labs, case studies, online activities, and simulations. *Due to the sensitive nature of this course, parents/guardians of enrolled students must sign a course permission form by the end of the first week of class. Embedded Honors option available. Students seeking honors recognition will need to meet all required course standards as well as complete additional assessments outside of class.
courses.prerequisites: Physical Science & Life Science

courses.description: Criminalistics is the application of science to those criminal and civil laws that are enforced by police agencies in a criminal justice system. This course is strongly recommended for students interested in pursuing a career in the medical or law enforcement field. It involves all areas of science including biology, anatomy, chemistry, physics, and earth science with an emphasis on complex reasoning and critical thinking. Specific topics will include: Hair Analysis, Fibers and Textiles, Forensic Botany, Handwriting Analysis, Forgery, and Counterfeiting, Glass Evidence, Casts and Impressions, Tool Marks, Firearms and Ballistics, Forensic Psychology, & Coroner’s Report. Students will engage in lectures, labs, case studies, online activities, and simulations. *Due to the sensitive nature of this course, parents/guardians of enrolled students must sign a course permission form by the end of the first week of class. Embedded Honors option available. Students seeking honors recognition will need to meet all required course standards as well as complete additional assessments outside of class.
courses.prerequisites: Physical Science, Life Science & Forensic Science

courses.description: This is a science elective, college preparatory course for those students who want to learn more about the human body and/or are interested in pursuing a career in the health sciences including nursing, athletic training and physical therapy. This course explores the structure and workings of the human machine with emphasis on the relationships between the skeletal, muscular, skin and nervous systems. The course includes some practical medical skills training in diagnosing patients, dissection to study the structure and function of various organs and tissues, as well as investigations to explore the body’s systems. Embedded Honors option available. Students seeking honors recognition will need to meet all required course standards as well as complete additional assessments outside of class.
courses.prerequisites: Physical Science & Life Science

courses.description: Discover how wildlife and ecosystems are interconnected and how to protect them. We will focus on what it’s like to think and work like a wildlife biologist. In this course, students explore wildlife and ecosystems using real scientific tools, in-class research, hands-on investigations, and field-based learning. With a strong focus on Vermont’s local ecosystems, students study animal and plant identification, animal life cycles, habitats, population dynamics, and conservation issues while connecting these concepts to ecosystems around the world. Students gain practical experience with field and observation techniques used by wildlife scientists and engage in place-based activities that build strong science and critical-thinking skills. The course also explores how human decisions, cultural values, and policies influence wildlife management at local, state, and national levels. By taking a whole-ecosystem approach, students learn how animals, habitats, and people are all connected. This course is perfect for students who enjoy learning outdoors, are curious about wildlife, ecology, and the natural world, and want to explore careers in environmental science, conservation, or natural resources.
courses.prerequisites: Physical Science & Life Science

courses.description: Science of Engineering is a hands-on course for students who are curious about the science behind the technologies and infrastructure of our world. Students will explore how the application of science, technology, and mathematics can solve problems through the engineering design process. The course will use a variety of design software, STEAM Lab equipment, and tools to explore processes used by engineers to identify and solve problems and a variety of challenges. Our work will use the engineering design process to define a problem, brainstorm solutions, develop prototypes, and iterate on their designs. The course will provide opportunities to develop the skills necessary to be a contributing member of any design team using science skills, design thinking, collaboration, communication, preparedness, and presenting work for a target audience. This course may be repeated if the student wants to continue building their engineering skills. Embedded honors option available.
courses.prerequisites: Physical Science & Life Science

courses.description: STEAM Design Fundamentals is a hands-on course that integrates the components of Science and Technology through Engineering and Artistic design all based on Mathematical elements. It will introduce students to the processes of critical thinking, analysis, and collaboration. In this course, students will explore different digital technologies to develop a set of STEAM skills and competencies for college, career, and life. Students will be presented with design challenges that will help prepare students to become problem solvers, innovators, creators, and collaborators. Upon completion of this course, proficient students will understand how to use the design cycle and apply it to future learning. This course may be repeated If the student wants to continue building their STEAM Design skills. Embedded Honors option available. Students seeking honors recognition will need to meet all required course standards as well as complete additional assessments outside of class.
courses.prerequisites: Physical Science & Life Science

courses.description: AP chemistry is a year long class that is equivalent to one semester of an undergraduate general chemistry course. At the end of the year, students can take the AP chemistry exam to earn college credit at certain universities. This course covers the basic properties of matter, molecular properties, chemical reactions, the kinetics of reactions, equilibrium reactions, thermodynamics, and acid/base reactions. Students are expected to have taken algebra 2 and the regular high school chemistry course to be successful. This is considered a difficult course that will require students to regularly do homework, use class time effectively, and attend outside class time. AP chemistry is a wonderful introduction to this subject for students interested in medicine, various engineering disciplines, and the sciences that explore the natural world through a mathematical lens such as chemistry, physics, geology, astronomy, etc. Students are required to take the AP Chemistry Exam in May.
courses.prerequisites: Physical Science, Life Science, Algebra II

courses.description: This year-long, rigorous course is designed for highly motivated students interested in a deeper, college level inquiry into biology. This includes topics in microbiology, biochemistry, genetics, evolution, and ecology. Students are expected to complete textbook reading at home in order to come to class prepared to engage with the topics, and complete a summer homework assignment before the beginning of the course. This course is strongly recommended for students interested in pursuing careers in medicine, life science, forensics, and related fields. Students are required to take the AP Biology Exam in May.
courses.prerequisites: Physical Science & Life Science

courses.description: Modern World History is a survey course in which students will explore major themes and essential questions about human civilizations over a broad period of time across the globe. As students explore achievements and conflicts in world history, they read and write extensively based on assigned primary and secondary sources and their own research. They analyze and evaluate historical information and present it in a variety of ways including historical investigation, research, writing, and discussions. Instruction will focus on building skills in reading, writing, research and historical thinking.

This course focuses on personal financial planning, which includes income and asset protection, income, investment, money management, and spending and credit management. The course is designed to help the learner make wise spending, saving, and credit decisions and to make effective use of income to achieve life-loing personal financial success.

Modern World History is a survey course in which students will explore major themes and essential questions about human civilizations over a broad period of time across the globe. As students explore achievements and conflicts in world history, they read and write extensively based on assigned primary and secondary sources and their own research. They analyze and evaluate historical information and present it in a variety of ways including historical investigation, research, writing, discussions, and role-play. Instruction will be scaffolded to meet student needs and will focus on building skills in reading, skills, research, and historical thinking.
courses.prerequisites: Placement by the History Department
courses.notes: Intended Grade Level: 10, 11, 12 students who need World History credit

courses.description: Modern U.S. History is a survey course that examines the history of the United States from the Post Civil War era to the present. Political, military, scientific, and social developments are typically included as part of the historical overview. This course will refine critical thinking and reading, writing, research and study skills. Independent reading and writing assignments will be assigned regularly, and a research paper is required. *Students must produce a proficient research project to receive credit for the class.
courses.prerequisites: 10th grade with Successful completion of World History

courses.description: Civics is the study of United States government and citizenship. Students will investigate the foundations and purposes of government at the federal, state, and local levels, along with understanding how Americans interact with their government on a daily basis, and vice versa. Students will examine the rights, duties, and responsibilities of a citizen at each level and participate in an authentic, inquiry based culminating activity. *Students must produce a proficient Active Citizen Interview Project to receive credit for the class.
courses.prerequisites: 10th grade with successful completion of US History. 11th-12th grade students have taken all required history courses (World History and U.S. History), or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval

courses.description: This course addresses Vermont and its history from settlement to today. Topics of study will include major events such as Abenaki, Settlement, Statehood, the Civil War, the Great Depression, Barre history, and the role of ordinary people and heroes in the state's heritage.
courses.prerequisites: 10th grade with successful completion of US History. 11th-12th grade students have taken all required history courses (Freshman Humanities and U.S. History), or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval

courses.description: This course explores the study of human relationships and interaction. Concepts include culture, cultural variations, norms and values, socialization process, status, classes and mobility, social institutions and social problems. Social science research techniques and critical thinking skills are stressed. Reading and writing assignments will be substantial and challenging.
courses.prerequisites: 10th grade with successful completion of US History. 11th-12th grade students have taken all required history courses (World History and U.S. History), or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval

courses.description: This course surveys the causes and effects of World War II in the European and Pacific theaters from the beginning of the conflict through the surrender of the Axis powers and the early stages of the Cold War. Through the use of primary and secondary sources, students analyze social, political, and military implications of one of the most devastating and transformational periods in human history. Students learn through a variety of individual and group activities and projects.
courses.prerequisites: 10th grade with successful completion of US History. 11th-12th grade students have taken all required history courses (Freshman Humanities and U.S. History), or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval.

courses.description: This class examines the military, political and diplomatic history of the war, as well as the context in which it was fought - the Cold War and the revolutionary changes of the 1960s themselves. Topics covered in this class will cover the early history and culture of Vietnam, the French involvement, Cold War tension and the nuclear standoff between the USSR and the USA, as well as early steps in American military involvement. We will also cover the United States at war in Vietnam and the mistakes made, the protest movement and the music of the time. We will conclude with the lessons learned as a result of American involvement in Vietnam, the memorials raised and how that conflict haunts American leaders even today.
courses.prerequisites: 10th grade with successful completion of US History. 11th-12th grade students have taken all required history courses (Freshman Humanities and U.S. History), or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval

courses.description: This course will examine efforts to systematically eliminate certain groups of people. Extensive attention will be paid to the Holocaust and Nazi Germany, while exploring genocides in other areas of the world, such as Rwanda and Cambodia. The course will consider the causes of genocide, the victims’ experience, the mindset of the perpetrators, and the international response, among other issues.
courses.prerequisites: 10th grade with successful completion of US History. 11th-12th grade students have taken all required history courses (World History and U.S. History), or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval

courses.description: This course focuses on the history of people who have pushed against the boundaries of history. Students will learn about the history of women and minorities, including African-American history and LGBTQ+. This course is designed to supplement U.S. History and focus on groups of people who were not satisfied with their place in history and decided to stand up and make changes.
courses.prerequisites: 10th grade with successful completion of US History. 11th-12th grade students have taken all required history courses (Freshman Humanities and U.S. History), or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval.

courses.description: This course is a study of different groups of people around the world and analyze how their geography has impacted their culture. Students will investigate how different geographic regions, resources, and scarcity has impacted peoples and cultures, way of life, perspectives and world events, and how people have adapted to their environments.
courses.prerequisites: 10th grade with successful completion of US History. 11th-12th grade students have taken all required history courses (Freshman Humanities and U.S. History), or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval

courses.description: This course explores issues in United States history specific to Native Americans. Topics of study include Native American culture prior to contact with Europeans, contact with and colonization by Europeans, Indian removal policies, reservation systems, the closing of the frontier, and current issues.
courses.prerequisites: 10th grade with successful completion of US History. 11th-12th grade students have taken all required history courses (World History and U.S. History), or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval

courses.description: Introduction to the Medieval World spanning the 5th century through the 15th century. In addition to studying the culture of Western Europe, the course will also look at Asian and Islamic influences at this time in order to gain an introductory view of important events, people and movements of the medieval era around the world as a whole. This course incorporates primary sources, interactive activities, medieval art, and writing projects as part of the exploration and study.
courses.prerequisites: 10th grade with successful completion of US History. 11th-12th grade students have taken all required history courses (World History and U.S. History), or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval

courses.description: Although attention will be devoted to the causes and long-term consequences of the Civil War, this class will focus primarily on the war years (1861-1865) with special emphasis on the military and technological aspects of the conflict. Four questions, long debated by historians, will receive close scrutiny: What caused the war? Why did the North win the war? Could the South have won? To what extent is the Civil War America's defining moment?
courses.prerequisites: 10th grade with successful completion of US History. 11th-12th grade students have taken all required history courses (World History and U.S. History), or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval

courses.description: This course offers a broad introduction to the study of Irish history and culture. Topics include: Irish storytelling throughout its history, the history of the conquest of Ireland and Irish independence movements; the role of the Irish language in culture; the famine and its social and political aftermath; the history of religious difference; the relationship between Britain and Ireland; and contemporary Ireland.
courses.prerequisites: 10th grade with successful completion of US History. 11th & 12th grade students have taken all required history courses (World History and U.S. History), or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval.

courses.description: This course will be self driven by student interest and will provide students with an intensive, interactive learning environment where they can actively engage with current research on a topic of their choice inspired by the National History Project Theme of the year. Students in this course choose a topic and dive deeply into the past by conducting extensive research in libraries, archives, and museums. They then present their conclusions and evidence through papers, exhibits, performances, documentaries, or websites. Research is an essential part of post secondary learning and this course will work to build those independent skills and ultimately prepare them for future academic research endeavors and professional applications of research knowledge. While this course is focused on social studies, the research skills learned are applicable to all disciplines.
courses.prerequisites: 10th grade with successful completion of US History. 11th-12th grade students have taken all required history courses (World History and U.S. History), or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval

courses.description: AP Economics provides students with a thorough understanding of the principles of economics. The course is divided between macroeconomics and microeconomics. Macro looks at the economic system as a whole, while Micro examines the principles of economics that apply to consumers and producers. In total, the course will examine the following areas: Supply and Demand, GDP, Fiscal and Monetary Policy, Comparative Advantage, Currency Exchange Rates, Resource Markets and Product Markets. There are AP tests in both Macroeconomics and Microeconomics. Successful completion of either Macro or Micro will earn financial literacy credit.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of World History and US History, or their equivalent or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval.

courses.description: AP Economics provides students with a thorough understanding of the principles of economics. The course is divided between macroeconomics and microeconomics. Macro looks at the economic system as a whole, while Micro examines the principles of economics that apply to consumers and producers. In total, the course will examine the following areas: Supply and Demand, GDP, Fiscal and Monetary Policy, Comparative Advantage, Currency Exchange Rates, Resource Markets and Product Markets. There are AP tests in both Macroeconomics and Microeconomics. Successful completion of either Macro or Micro will earn financial literacy credit.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of World History and US History, or their equivalent or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval.

courses.description: This course explores the government and politics in China, Iran, Mexico, Nigeria, Russia, and the United Kingdom. Throughout the course, students will learn how different governments solve similar problems and will gain a clear understanding of the comparative method by analyzing data and text-based sources, making comparisons and applications, and developing evidence-based arguments.
courses.prerequisites: Successful Completion of US History, Civics or AP US Government. Or with Teacher/Department Chair Approval.

courses.description: AP US History will cover the content and skills required for the AP exam, which all students are required to take in May. Students will use a college-level textbook and read and write extensively. The course will refine critical thinking techniques and expose students to alternate perspectives on history through print and visual media. The class will move at a quick pace and a considerable amount of independent work will be expected of students.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Humanities History and US History, or their equivalent or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval.

courses.description: AP United States Government and Politics will cover content for the AP exam and introduces students to key political ideas, institutions, policies, interactions, roles, and behaviors that characterize the political culture of the United States. The course examines politically significant concepts and themes, through which students learn to apply disciplinary reasoning to assess causes and consequences of political events, and interpret data to develop evidence-based arguments.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Humanities History and US History, or their equivalent or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval.

courses.description: This survey course explores the economic, political, cultural, and social developments in world history from the rise of civilization to 1500 CE in Asia, Africa, Europe, and the Americas. The course highlights geography, cultural and political movements, and human interactions that influenced the historical evolution of various world societies and their interrelationships within a global context.
courses.prerequisites: Acceptance to CCV as a Dual Enrollment Student. Students should show evidence of college readiness by earning 3.5 or higher in English 10, US History or their equivalent or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval. Note: this course has an attendance requirement.

courses.description: A survey of the basic issues, concepts, theories and methods of psychology. Students will increase their awareness of the scientific approach to understanding human behavior through a study of sensory processes, perception, emotion, motivation, intelligence, learning and personality formation.
courses.prerequisites: Acceptance to CCV as a Dual Enrollment Student. Students should show evidence of college readiness by earning 3.5 or higher in English 10, US History or their equivalent or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval. Note: this course has an attendance requirement.

courses.course_name: CCV Society and Environment in History
courses.description: An exploration of the response to environmental challenges by various societies in history and why societies fail and perish, or succeed and survive. Students will describe strategies employed by societies that survive environmental challenges and analyze the relationship and interaction between society and environment in the development of sustainable communities.
courses.prerequisites: Acceptance to CCV as a Dual Enrollment Student. Students should show evidence of college readiness by earning 3.5 or higher in English 10, US History or their equivalent or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval. Note: this course has an attendance requirement.

courses.description: This course is a survey of human growth and development throughout the life cycle including physical, cognitive, linguistic, ethical, and psychosocial dimensions. Students will identify and discuss issues in human growth and development arising from differences in gender, race, and socioeconomic status.
courses.prerequisites: Acceptance to CCV as a Dual Enrollment Student. Students should show evidence of college readiness by earning 3.5 or higher in English 10, US History or their equivalent or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval. Note: this course has an attendance requirement.

courses.description: This course will cover topics in military leadership, citizenship, interpersonal communications/relations, public speaking, written communications, and physical fitness, with emphasis in personal responsibility. Students will develop their leadership skills during class time through drill and ceremonies (D&C), and physical training (PT). Additional leadership opportunities are available outside the classroom. Students will experience a hands-on learning environment using a military model, with extensive intra-curricular service learning opportunities. Students are required to attend a weekly “formation” conducted at 0730 in the gym on the first school day each week, wearing the prescribed uniform. Additionally, students are required to participate in the Barre Veterans Day parade.

This course description is similar to LET1, however units are as follows: military drill, physical training, "You the people" (a citizenship-skills foundation of the American political system), creating the constitution, shaping American institutions, and practices for citizen roles in American democracy.

This advanced level course capitalizes on the training received in LET1 and LET2 to allow cadets to assume senior level non-commissioned officer and junior officer ranks in the cadet organization. The course reviews, reinforces and expands on each of the subject areas with emphasis on career development and the pursuit of higher education.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of LET 2

courses.description: Primary emphasis will be placed on the practical application of the cadet organization. Therefore, the LET4 year is structured to allow cadets to perform their assigned command or staff duties and act as a class instructor or assistant instructor for selected LET 1 through 3 subjects. Academic instruction for LET4 will consist of self-paced study, suggested readings, seminars, vignettes, case studies, and special assignments.
courses.prerequisites: Earn Partial Proficiency in LET 3

courses.description: These advanced level courses are available to cadets having successfully completed the program and who wish to continue to develop leadership and managerial skills in the program by becoming teacher assistants in the LET 1 through 4 classes. Students are expected to perform duties as assigned to include: special projects, tutoring, classroom instruction, coaching of the various extracurricular activities, and to act as cadet mentors.
courses.prerequisites: Permission of Instructor

courses.description: In this quarter-long elective course, students will be introduced to basic conversational French, focusing on the vocabulary and phrases they would most need if traveling to a French-speaking country or region. In addition, they will learn about French, African, Quebecois traditions, geography, and history. This course can be taken as a one-time exploratory elective or used as a springboard into the more formal study of the French language.

This course is for students with no exposure to French. Students are exposed to facets of language through mostly storytelling. With an online platform, students engage with the stories by using all the skills of reading, listening, speaking and writing. Interactive activities, music, videos, game play are used to reinforce the material. This is a highly social class where interpersonal exchanges and cooperative work and conversation with peers are practiced daily. Emphasis is on comprehension and application of the stories and questions in a variety of modes along with exposure to the culture of the French speaking world. Embedded Honors available.

This course is a continuation of French 1 storytelling and comprehensible input. It is designed for the student with a solid grasp of the fundamentals of French 1. Basic skills are reviewed before progressing into new material. Students learn more complicated grammatical concepts through the stories, acquire more essential vocabulary and continue to practice their reading, writing, listening, and speaking skills through interactive activities, games, projects and classwork. Emphasis is on asking and answering questions in order to create meaningful dialogue.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of French I or demonstrated proficiency

courses.description: A continuation of language acquisition, this course stresses more grammar, which is used in writing exercises and short compositions. It also focuses on acquiring language through storytelling but progressing to the past tense. New vocabulary is presented along with short stories and students use this in both oral and written expression. Speaking is emphasized at this level, with students being able to converse more spontaneously. Students make cultural connections through the online platform, stories, music, and authentic materials.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of French II or demonstrated proficiency

courses.description: Through more storytelling and comprehensible input, this is an accelerated and intensive course providing a more complete and thorough coverage of the French language, in which speaking proficiency, listening comprehension, vocabulary acquisition, reading, and writing are brought to a level enabling students to use the language actively in everyday situations. This course is especially designed for the student who has the capability to function at a higher level of language acquisition and is self-directed and highly motivated.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of French III or demonstrated proficiency

courses.description: This course is normally offered as an independent study. Students who attain this level of study are self-directed and motivated. Before beginning the course, students will outline the areas of culture, vocabulary and reading that they wish to explore. They will continue with more advanced grammar and use their studies to improve their writing in more complex projects and essays.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of French I, French II, French III, and French IV or demonstrated proficiency

courses.description: This course is for students with little to no exposure to the Spanish language. Listening, speaking, reading and writing will be the main focus in this class and will be practiced within thematic units. Students are exposed to the mechanics of the language through highly interactive activities, reading short dialogues, stories, Q+A practice and writing short responses. This is a highly social class where interpersonal exchanges and cooperative work and conversation with peers are practiced daily. Emphasis is on vocabulary acquisition, basic grammar skills, and being able to interact with others. Exposure to, research and awareness of the Spanish speaking world at large will help students become more globally minded citizens.

This course is a continuation of the work that has been covered in Spanish I. The main focus is being able to keep up with listening, speaking, reading and writing proficiencies. Students are expected to read and retell stories, easily converse in Spanish with peers using key verbs and vocabulary and be able to move through meaningful Q+A scenarios with peers on a daily basis. There will be a heavy focus on reading short stories, retelling these shared stories and listening. Writing will consist of short narratives and various comprehension activities. As in Spanish I, this is a highly social class where interpersonal exchanges and cooperative work and conversation with peers are practiced daily.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish I or demonstrated proficiency

courses.description: This course is a continuation of the work that has been covered in Spanish I and II. The main focus is being able to keep up with listening, speaking, reading and writing proficiencies in a more in-depth capacity with the language. Literacy is a strong focus in this class. This course stresses key vocabulary acquisition as well as more complex grammar that will be used in various writing exercises and compositions, as well as in shared exchanges between peers and speech. Reading includes short cultural stories and the ability to engage in more lengthy readings and dialogues. Speaking is emphasized at this level, with students being able to converse spontaneously with key language structures. Students will continue to make cultural connections through films, music and authentic materials.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish II or demonstrated proficiency

courses.description: Through more conversation, readings, storytelling and comprehensible input, this is an accelerated and intensive course providing a more complete and thorough coverage of the Spanish language, in which speaking proficiency, listening comprehension,vocabulary acquisition, reading, and writing are brought to a level enabling students to use the language actively and spontaneously in everyday situations. This course is especially designed for the student who has the capability to function at a higher level of language acquisition and is self-directed and highly motivated.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish III or demonstrated proficiency

courses.description: Students who attain this level of study are self-directed and motivated. Before beginning the course, students should be able to outline the areas of culture, vocabulary and reading that they wish to explore within the Spanish speaking world. Self-directed projects and research along with accelerated language acquisition will be a heavy focus during this course. Students will continue to be expected to gain, use and maneuver more advanced grammar and use their independent and collaborative studies to improve both their speaking and writing in more complex dialogues, projects and essays.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish IV or demonstrated proficiency

courses.description: This hands-on course introduces students to the fundamentals of art-making through exploration, creativity, and self expression. Students will learn foundational skills in drawing, painting, sculpture, and mixed media while developing an understanding of the elements of art and principles of design. Through guided projects and open-ended challenges, students will experiment with materials and techniques, engage in creative problem solving, and reflect on their artistic process. Emphasis is placed on fostering a supportive studio environment where students are encouraged to take creative risks, share ideas, and appreciate diverse perspectives.

As an introduction to digital photographic techniques, students will use Adobe Lightroom throughout the course to produce and edit their photographs. Emphasis will be placed on the elements and principles of design and how they contribute to strong composition in photography. Students have the opportunity to learn the mechanics of digital photography, lighting techniques and digital image manipulation. Students will be required to take photographs outside of class time.

Advanced Art is an upper-level studio course designed for students who are ready to deepen their artistic voice, technical skill, and creative independence. Through sustained investigation, students explore a variety of media - including drawing, painting, printmaking, sculpture, mixed media, and digital tools - while developing personal themes and concepts in their work. Students engage in increasingly rigorous studio practice, including sketchbook development, collaborative critiques, and reflective writing. A key focus of the course is portfolio development. Students will produce a cohesive body of work suitable for college applications, exhibitions, or personal artistic growth. This class fosters a supportive and challenging environment where each student pushes their skills, takes ownership of their process, and discovers deeper meaning in their artmaking.
courses.prerequisites: Art Studio Introduction and/or Teacher Approval

courses.description: Since the invention of the motion picture humans have been fascinated by the experience of cinema. While many of us carry a video camera everywhere we go, that doesn’t mean that we are using them to their fullest potential. This quarter-long class will introduce you to the filmmaking process. Students will learn strategies for creating stories by shooting, editing and manipulating sound to create short films.
courses.prerequisites: None

courses.description: Clay + Fire = Stone. The ceramic process has been used by humans for over 20,000 years. Whether you prefer to make functional pottery or decorative sculpture, Ceramics will allow you to build spatial reasoning and fine motor skills as you form, refine and complete artworks. Students will use a variety of tools including (but not limited to): extrusion, firing, glazing, hand building, modeling and wheel throwing. Students are expected to create a body of finished work and participate in either the Winter or Spring SHS Art Show as a requirement for achieving Proficiency. This course may be repeated If the student wants to continue building their skills.

3D printing, laser cutting and digital illustration are a few of the media that you will have the opportunity to learn in I.D.E.A. & Craft. If you prefer traditional, analog artmaking carving foam, wood and stone are options for your creative expression as well. Students will be able to embrace their creativity in whichever mode they prefer in this quarter long course.

Dive into the rich and versatile world of fiber arts in this engaging and hands-on course. Students will learn a variety of techniques such as embroidery, felting, crocheting, and sewing while exploring the cultural and historical significance of textiles across the globe. This course emphasizes creativity, craftsmanship, and self-expression as students create unique, functional, and decorative pieces. Open to all skill levels.

This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental principles and techniques of drawing. Through a series of hands-on projects, students will explore various drawing mediums, such as pencil, charcoal, ink, and pastels. Emphasis will be placed on developing observational skills, understanding proportions, shading techniques, perspective, and composition. Students will study both traditional and contemporary approaches to drawing, with opportunities to experiment and express their individual creativity. Critiques and discussions will foster a collaborative studio environment, encouraging students to analyze and reflect on their own work and that of their peers. By the end of the course, students will have gained a solid foundation in drawing and created a portfolio to showcase their artistic development. This course is open to all skill levels and aims to inspire a lifelong appreciation for the art of drawing.

Explore the dynamic possibilities of mixed media in this hands-on studio course. Students will experiment with combining various materials and techniques, such as drawing, painting, collage, printmaking, and found objects to create unique works of art. Emphasis will be placed on creative problem-solving, personal expression, and the interplay of texture, color, and form. Through guided projects, open-studio time, and critique, students will develop their technical skills, artistic vision, and understanding of communal studio practices. No prior experience necessary- just curiosity and willingness to create!

The Spaulding Band meets every day during our AM block. The band is open to all students. Prior experience is not required. Students will gain experience in both marching and concert band settings. Band members will also work independently on developing their skills and abilities at their own pace. Band members are expected to perform at 2 concerts, all home football games and local parades and Pep Band Events. Embedded Honors available.
courses.notes: Credit stated per semester; course length not stated

courses.description: This course meets everyday during AM block. Chorus is open to all students with a desire to learn to sing. Prior singing experience is not required. Students will gain exposure to a wide variety of styles and genres of music including classical, pop, broadway, folk, and world music. Students will learn the fundamentals of singing, sight reading, and music notation. Attendance at public performances that take place outside of the school day is expected. Embedded Honors available.
courses.notes: Credit stated per semester; course length not stated

courses.description: The Popular Music Ensemble performs popular music, including, but not limited to Blues, Country, R&B, Hip Hop, Funk and Soul Music. Rehearsals are conducted as coaching sessions, where both instrumentalists and singers perform together and blend sounds of musical instruments including piano, guitar, bass, percussion, wind instruments and MIDI devices. Students will be expected to participate in the written preparation of original and arranged music. This class is designed to provide students with a hands-on learning experience of music in a non-traditional format.
courses.prerequisites: Teacher recommendation required prior to enrollment.

courses.description: This is an honors level class. Students will refine the basic skills learned in Chorus. This class is ideal for students looking for more challenging music and individual attention. In addition to more advanced repertoire, students will work on individual vocal development, sight-reading, and further developing their literacy in music theory. Students are expected to attend multiple performances throughout the semester including Baccalaureate and SHS graduation.
courses.prerequisites: Concurrent enrollment in Band or Chorus, recommendation or invitation by instructor

courses.description: This course is designed for music students who wish to gain an understanding of the form, structure, and sound of music. This course will provide a background in the basics of music and how it is organized. Topics include reading bass and treble clef, intervals, scales, triads, rhythms, and more. Students will be taught music theory and offered practice in theory concepts through computer assisted compositions.

This course is for the beginning guitar student with or without previous music experience. The class will consist of a survey of musical styles with emphasis on note reading. Limited to 15 students, priority is given to juniors and seniors.
courses.prerequisites: Students are urged to supply their own acoustic guitar. If this is not a possibly, the Music Department does have a limited number of guitars for student use.

courses.description: This class is designed for students that have successfully completed Beginning Guitar (FNA 302) or have previous experience with Guitar playing. Students will receive guidance and direction in solving problems related to playing the guitar on an intermediate level and will learn many of the different styles, skills, and techniques required to become a successful musician.

This course is designed for students who wish to gain an understanding and appreciation of World music. This course will provide a background in the techniques and traditions of World drumming. The class will be taught aurally and students will not read music. No prior drumming experience is required, nor is the ability to read music. A willingness to try new things and have fun is required! Course limited to 15 students.

This Course traces the development of American popular music from its roots in the blues, through jazz and early rock and roll, continuing through contemporary styles of rock music. It will involve lecture, listening, discussion, student research, presentations and written work. Assessments are largely project based.

This course is designed for the beginning music student who is interested in developing basic piano and music reading skills. No previous experience required. Students will learn the concepts and fundamentals needed to play piano. This class operates largely on an individual basis. The curriculum is developed in a sequential manner - moving from simple to more complex concepts. There is ample opportunity for practice and review in order for the student to gain understanding and appropriate skill development. Weekly performances in class are the primary means of assessing proficiency and skill development. Performances are made only to the instructor and not to the entire class. Limited to 15 students.

This class explores the ways we experience and interact with music in our lives and how it can impact us. The general topics we will focus on in this course are music in our everyday lives, how music affects our brain, and music in film, as well as creating our own music using online software. There is no performance component to this class, but this class is an opportunity to be creative. Assessments are largely project based.

Students will enjoy a very welcoming and non-competitive atmosphere during this experience. The class will focus on health, fitness and wellness implementation to create a symbiotic and harmonious relationship with the mind, body and soul. Students will have the opportunity to take part in breathing exercises, embracing nature, and wellness goal planning. The overall goal of this course is to create an alternative to a more traditional physical education class setting and allow students to embark on a personal journey toward holistic health and well-being. This class will focus on the dimensions of wellness which include, but are not limited to, physical, social, emotional, spiritual, intellectual, environmental, and occupational wellness.
courses.prerequisites: Wellness and/or Introductory PE

courses.description: This section is the prerequisite course for all other PE courses. Students will gain understanding of games by participating in a variety of recreational sports, lifetime activities, and non-traditional games. 3-4 days per week students will experience games like badminton, floor hockey, cornhole, and wiffleball where they will work towards better understanding game play concepts, rules, and strategies as well as motor skill development/refinement. In addition to learning games, students will also gain an understanding of and participation in basic fitness programs focused on the ‘5 elements of fitness’(Cardio, Muscle Strength, Muscle Endurance, Flexibility and Body Composition). 1-2 days per week students will experience genres of fitness like Yoga, Performance Training and various Cardio & Resistance Training methods.

Want to get stronger, feel better, and improve your overall fitness? In this Personal Fitness class, you'll get the chance to set your own fitness goals and work toward achieving them in a fun and supportive environment. You'll participate in a variety of workouts, including strength training, HIIT, and circuit training, to build muscle, boost endurance, and increase energy. On other days, enjoy recreational sports, yoga, stretching, and recovery techniques that help you stay balanced and healthy. Whether you're new to fitness or looking to take your training to the next level, this class will help you feel your best, both physically and mentally.
courses.prerequisites: Introductory Physical Education

courses.description: Get ready for action and teamwork in the Team Games class! This course is designed for students who love playing sports and working together as a team. You’ll have the chance to compete in a variety of team-based games like basketball, soccer, volleyball, and more. Throughout the class, you'll develop your skills in strategy, communication, and leadership while staying active and having fun.
courses.prerequisites: Introductory Physical Education

courses.description: If you love sports that involve strategy, teamwork, and quick reflexes, the Net Games class is for you! In this class, you’ll play and improve your skills in exciting net game sports like: volleyball, badminton, and pickleball. You'll learn the rules, techniques, and strategies needed to succeed in each game while staying active and having fun. Whether you're a beginner or have some experience, this class offers a great opportunity to improve your hand-eye coordination, communication, and sportsmanship.
courses.prerequisites: Introductory Physical Education

courses.description: This honors level PE class will offer the opportunity to teach and mentor students that are part of the life skills program in a variety of physical activities.The mentor's responsibility will be to guide, assist and teach their partner through a variety of skills and strategies during activities. Emphasizing teamwork, respect for others, problem solving will also play a strong role in the relationship between the mentor and the mentee when participating in activities.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of 2 PE classes (Intro and another), Proficient or higher for final grade.

courses.description: This a required, semester-long course focuses on developing skills for lifelong personal health. These skills include analyzing influences, accessing health resources, interpersonal communication, advocacy, decision making, goal setting, and practicing health behaviors. Health topics include disease prevention, relationships, alcohol and other drugs, nutrition, and stress management.

This semester-long course focuses on developing skills for lifelong personal health. These skills include analyzing influences, accessing health resources, interpersonal communication, advocacy, decision making, goal setting, and practicing health behaviors. Health topics include disease prevention, relationships, alcohol and other drugs, nutrition, and stress management. This course is designed for students who have not completed the first-year Wellness course. Preferred level is 11th and 12th grades.

This quarter-long course introduces students to the fundamental concepts of nutrition, focusing on a weight-inclusive approach that prioritizes health and well-being. Students will explore how different nutrients affect the body and learn how to make informed choices based on personal needs, activity levels, and health goals. This course encourages students to develop a healthy relationship with food, promoting physical and mental well-being all while exploring the physical, emotional, and cultural importance of food.
courses.prerequisites: Health or Wellness

courses.description: This course prepares novice drivers to drive safely on America’s highways and empowers teens to manage high risk situations using the most appropriate highway user attitudes, responsible driving skills, and traffic safety principles available. Course topics include the driving task, zone control, reference points, driving in urban traffic, rural areas, and on expressways, handling emergencies and adverse conditions, insurance and liability, legal issues, and the effects of driver impairment on driving. This program requires students to show respect and tolerance.
courses.prerequisites: A valid Learner's Permit prior to the first class and Sophomore status.

courses.description: This course will cover core concepts of maple syrup production. Maple syrup production is a very important aspect of Vermont life and history. Every year in the early spring people of all ages find their way to the woods to tap trees, collect sap, and participate in the great tradition of producing maple syrup. Vermont is the largest maple syrup producer in the United States and maple is an essential industry from a historical, cultural, agricultural, and economic perspective. As the industry continues to grow, it creates potential employment opportunities for people of all ages, including recent high school graduates.

The class will spend much of its time in the field learning how to and installing maple tubing. The students will learn how to operate basic tubing installation tools once completing basic training and completing a basic OSHA course. Once tubing is installed the class will gather data on the 3 tubing systems sap yield based on environmental conditions and the weather. When the students are not in the field students will compile and analyze the data to determine a theory on which system yields the most sap and why. The second component of the course will involve multiple site visits to large sugaring operations around the state. While on these site visits students will observe techniques used to gather and process maple sap into maple syrup. These large scale operations will also provide the students with the opportunity to view and understand the business/marketing side of the Maple Industry.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Maple Program Class

courses.description: This is an introductory course on Work Based Learning that enables students to gain the necessary skills and knowledge of being a part of the workforce. Topics will include Career Readiness & Professionalism in the Workplace, workplace safety, and exposure to various work settings through the Central Vermont area. Students will also have the chance to participate in an activity in the nonprofit sector, and spend the remaining semester in a Work Based Learning opportunity off-site.
courses.prerequisites: A valid driver’s license and access to reliable and insured transportation. If interested in a medical placement, additional requirements are needed. For some placements, one must be 18 years of age prior to placement.

courses.description: Work Based Learning will be offered in the format of a semester class helping students make clear, informed choices about their futures by learning about what education, experiences, and training (E2T) they can obtain with a post secondary institution, such as a 2 or 4 year college/university. This has been especially meaningful for students who may seek out a post-secondary education at a technical or community college, students who are seeking a four year college education and ask “WHY college?”, or for students who may be interested in exploring a particular career immediately after high school.

This elective is a semester-long course (internship) that enables students to gain practical skills and knowledge about a particular field, along with learning about the aspects of a workplace. It allows students to gain first hand knowledge and determine if this particular career/field is still of interest to them. Components of the course include: preparation and professionalism in the workforce, climate and confidentiality, required written assignments, training agreement, evaluations, and a final product, along with meeting the standards outlined in the curriculum map
courses.prerequisites: Earned Proficiency in WBL200A. A valid driver’s license and access to reliable and insured transportation. If interested in a medical placement, additional requirements are needed. For some placements, one must be 18 years of age prior to placement.

courses.description: Opportunity for Junior and Senior students to connect academic learning to careers and employment by participating in job shadows, employee panels and unpaid work experiences within the Central Vermont community.
An Opportunity for students to pursue a particular discipline under the supervision and guidance of a certified teacher at Spaulding High School.

courses.department: Early College / Dual Enrollment / Online Learning
courses.description: Concurrent courses are Community College of Vermont (CCV) approved courses, taught by a Spaulding High School teacher, and during the regular high school day. A Dual Enrollment voucher is required to be used to access this course (examples: English Comp, Contemporary Literature, & Introduction to Psychology). Students will need to meet CCV's requirements in order to access these courses.

courses.department: Early College / Dual Enrollment / Online Learning
courses.description: Juniors and Seniors have the opportunity to utilize two Dual Enrollment vouchers during their high school years. This program allows for such students to enroll in college classes for credit, awarded both through SHS and the chosen college/university, at no tuition cost.

courses.department: Early College / Dual Enrollment / Online Learning
courses.description: Early College is a full year rigorous alternative to the traditional senior year of high school. Students enroll in college level courses, typically taking four to five courses per semester, which allows them to complete both their senior year of high school and their first year of college simultaneously tuition free. While tuition is covered, families/caregivers and students are responsible for associated fees required by the participating institution. Several institutions offer Early College programs including Norwich University, Community College of Vermont, and Vermont State University. Students interested in Early College should meet with their school counselor and 504/IEP case manager to determine whether the program is an appropriate fit. It is recommended that students begin exploring Early College options during the first semester of their junior year as application deadlines vary by institution.
courses.provider: Norwich University, Community College of Vermont, Vermont State University

courses.department: Early College / Dual Enrollment / Online Learning
courses.description: An opportunity for students to take online courses through Virtual High School. This option can be relevant for students looking for classes not offered at SHS, for areas of scheduling conflict with required courses, or to supplement a student's schedule outside of the regular school day.

Opportunity for students who are enrolled in a technical center program who would like to enroll in college courses in their particular technical field. This is similar to Dual Enrollment, in that there is no tuition cost, but is only for students of CVCC
